nameStory: The 'max' in max chrysanthemum comes from 'maximum,' referring to this daisy's impressively large flower heads that can stretch up to 4 inches across. It's essentially the 'supersized' version of its smaller cousin, the common oxeye daisy. The chrysanthemum part of the name reflects its membership in the huge daisy family, though it's not a true chrysanthemum.
description: Max chrysanthemum is a robust perennial wildflower that looks like a classic white daisy on steroids. It produces large, cheerful flower heads with bright white petals radiating around a sunny yellow center, sitting atop sturdy stems that can reach 2-3 feet tall. The plant forms clumps of dark green, lance-shaped leaves and blooms throughout much of the summer. Think of it as the garden-variety daisy's bigger, showier sibling.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large white daisy-like flower heads up to 4 inches across with 15-30 crisp white petals surrounding a bright yellow center that feels slightly bumpy to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Dark green, lance-shaped leaves with toothed edges that feel somewhat leathery and have a slightly waxy surface when rubbed between fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sturdy, upright stems 2-3 feet tall that feel firm and hollow when gently squeezed, growing in clumps from a spreading root system

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, ribbed seeds with no fluffy white parachute (unlike dandelions), developing in the yellow center after petals fade

habitat: Max chrysanthemum thrives in sunny, well-drained locations like meadows, roadsides, field edges, and disturbed soils throughout New England. You'll often find it in gardens where it has escaped cultivation, along with other non-native wildflowers like chicory and Queen Anne's lace. It prefers full sun and tolerates poor soils better than many native plants.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as bright green basal rosettes, with stems beginning to elongate by late spring. No flowers yet, but the robust leaf growth is already noticeable.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August, with large white flower heads opening in succession. This is when the plant is most easily identified and at its showiest.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, gradually producing seeds. Leaves begin to yellow and die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back to ground level, leaving dried stems and seed heads that may persist. Look for dead rosettes of leaves at the base.

funFact: Despite being called a chrysanthemum, max chrysanthemum is actually more closely related to the oxeye daisy than to the fall mums you see in garden centers - it's a case of mistaken identity that stuck in the common name!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its smaller relative, the oxeye daisy, but max chrysanthemum has noticeably larger flower heads (up to 4 inches vs. 1-2 inches) and more robust, taller stems. Memory trick: 'Max' means maximum size - if it's a really big white daisy, it's probably the max chrysanthemum.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the 'chrysanthemum' name fool you - this isn't the same as the colorful fall mums sold at garden centers. That's a completely different plant genus (Chrysanthemum), while max chrysanthemum belongs to the Leucanthemum genus along with oxeye daisies.
compareHints: Max chrysanthemum is basically the big brother of oxeye daisy (Leucanthemum vulgare) - same family resemblance but supersized. While oxeye daisy has flower heads typically 1-2 inches across, max chrysanthemum blooms can reach up to 4 inches. Max chrysanthemum also tends to be taller and more robust overall, with thicker stems and larger leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Oxeye daisy is much smaller than its relative max chrysanthemum (Shasta daisy), with flowers typically 2 inches across versus 3-4 inches.
